clinicalPearls: A selective deficiency of pituitary ACTH secretion with preservation of the other anterior pituitary hormones, causing secondary adrenal insufficiency
Presents with fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia, but without hyperpigmentation because ACTH is low, unlike in primary adrenal insufficiency

Aldosterone secretion is preserved because it is renin-angiotensin driven, so severe salt wasting and hyperkalaemia are not typical, though hyponatraemia can still occur from cortisol-deficiency-related water retention
It can be an overlooked cause of unexplained hyponatraemia or recurrent hypoglycaemia
Causes include lymphocytic hypophysitis (including autoimmune and, increasingly, immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced disease), congenital TBX19 (TPIT) or POMC defects, and idiopathic disease
Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy is now an important acquired cause and should be sought in the drug history
Diagnosis rests on low or inappropriately normal ACTH with low cortisol and an impaired cortisol response to stimulation, with the other pituitary axes intact
Treatment is glucocorticoid replacement, and mineralocorticoid is not required
reference.pathophysiology: Isolated ACTH deficiency is characterised by impaired secretion of corticotropin from the pituitary corticotrophs while the other anterior pituitary hormones remain intact, resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoid deficiency but preserved mineralocorticoid function. Acquired cases most often reflect autoimmune corticotroph destruction as in lymphocytic hypophysitis, including that triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs; congenital cases result from mutations in TBX19 (TPIT), a transcription factor essential for pro-opiomelanocortin expression in corticotrophs, or from defects in pro-opiomelanocortin processing. Because aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system rather than ACTH, salt and potassium handling is largely maintained, and the absence of ACTH excess explains the lack of hyperpigmentation.
additionalDifferentials: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with high ACTH, hyperpigmentation and mineralocorticoid deficiency
Panhypopituitarism or multiple pituitary hormone deficiency
Suppression of the axis by exogenous glucocorticoids, the commonest cause of secondary adrenal insufficiency
Other causes of hyponatraemia such as SIADH or hypothyroidism
Sepsis or another cause of hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Paired morning serum cortisol and plasma ACTH, showing low or inappropriately normal ACTH with low cortisol
Dynamic testing of cortisol reserve, such as a short synacthen test or, in specialist settings, insulin tolerance or CRH testing
Assessment of the other anterior pituitary axes to confirm the deficiency is isolated, covering thyroid, gonadal, growth hormone and prolactin function
Serum sodium and glucose for hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia
Review of glucocorticoid and immune checkpoint inhibitor drug exposure
Pituitary MRI to look for hypophysitis or another structural lesion
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and collapse, especially during intercurrent illness
New ACTH deficiency after starting an immune checkpoint inhibitor
Failure to increase glucocorticoid at times of physiological stress
reference.prognosis: Excellent with appropriate glucocorticoid replacement and sick-day dosing education; the main danger is unrecognised or under-treated adrenal crisis, and checkpoint-inhibitor-induced deficiency is typically permanent and requires lifelong replacement.
pitfalls: Expecting hyperpigmentation and hyperkalaemia and so missing the diagnosis, since these belong to primary insufficiency
Attributing hyponatraemia to SIADH without checking cortisol
Overlooking immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy as a cause
Failing to give stress-dose glucocorticoid and crisis-prevention advice
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Adrenal Insufficiency
management: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone to correct cortisol deficiency; mineralocorticoid replacement is unnecessary because aldosterone secretion is preserved
Sick-day rules with glucocorticoid dose escalation during intercurrent illness and parenteral steroid for vomiting or major physiological stress
Emergency treatment of adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation
Patient education, a steroid emergency card and provision of injectable hydrocortisone for home use
Review immune checkpoint inhibitor and exogenous glucocorticoid exposure as precipitants, continuing replacement as checkpoint-induced deficiency is usually permanent
Monitor clinical response and periodically assess the other anterior pituitary axes to confirm the deficiency remains isolated
Endocrinology referral for diagnostic confirmation and long-term supervision
